title: Queensberry and the Ring
bigQuestion: How did written rules turn bare-knuckle prize fights into gloved boxing, and why do schools, clubs and town gyms treat boxing so differently?

story.title: Two Books on Two Desks
story.kicker: One desk holds a boxing rule book from 1867; another holds a school sports handbook.
paragraphs: On a library desk lies a small printed page from London. It lists twelve short rules for boxing. It is dated 1867. It asks for gloves, rounds of three minutes and a rest of one minute between them.

On a desk in an Illinois high school office lies a thick handbook. It is from the Illinois High School Association, the IHSA, which began in 1900. It lists the sports that schools may play for state titles. Wrestling is on the list. Boxing is not.
Across town, a boxing gym has a ring, heavy bags and a sign-up sheet. Young people train there after school. The gym follows rules too, but they come from a different group, not from the school.
This chapter asks how the rule book on the first desk came to be. Then it asks why boxing lives in clubs, newspaper tournaments and town gyms more than in school gyms.
story.think: Why might a sport have rules from one group in a school and rules from another group in a town gym?

lessons.title: A Bronze Boxer in Rome
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient Greek and Roman boxers wrapped their hands in leather straps, and a bronze statue shows one at rest.
reading: Greek writers said boxing joined the ancient Olympic Games in 688 BCE. Greek boxers did not wear soft gloves. They wrapped their hands and wrists in long leather *straps*. There were no rounds. A bout went on until one boxer gave up or could not go on.
In 1885, workers digging in Rome found a bronze statue of a seated boxer. Today it is called the Boxer at Rest. It was made more than 2,000 years ago. It is in the National Museum of Rome.

The statue shows leather straps wound around the boxer's hands. It also shows a broken nose, cuts and swollen ears. Artists made the *injuries* on purpose. The statue is evidence that ancient boxing hurt the people who did it.

words.d: a long strip of leather; ancient boxers wound straps around their hands
harm to the body, such as a cut or a broken bone

lessons.title: Broughton's Rules of 1743
lessons.mainIdea: In 1743, the London boxer Jack Broughton wrote seven rules, the first written rules for English boxing.
reading: In the 1700s, boxing matches in England were called *prize fights*. Two men fought with bare fists for money. Crowds bet on the winner. Many towns saw the fights as disorder, and they were often against the law.

Jack Broughton was a champion boxer in London. He ran a building where fights were held, called an amphitheater. In 1743 he wrote seven rules for fights there. One rule gave a fallen boxer 30 seconds to come back to the middle. Another said no one could hit a man who was down.

Broughton also taught boxing to rich young men. For practice, he used padded gloves called *mufflers*. Real prize fights stayed bare-knuckle. Broughton's rules guided English prize fights for nearly 100 years.

words.d: a bare-knuckle boxing match fought for money, common in England in the 1700s and 1800s
padded gloves Jack Broughton used for practice in the 1740s
seven rules for boxing written by Jack Broughton in London in 1743

look.title: One of Broughton's Rules
look.text: No one may hit his opponent when he is down. A boxer who is on his knees counts as down.
look.cite: Jack Broughton, Rules to be observed in all battles on the stage, London, 1743 (retold in plain English)
look.prompt: Why would a rule about a fallen boxer be one of the first rules someone wrote down?

check.q: Who wrote the first written rules for English boxing?
check.why: Jack Broughton wrote seven rules in London in 1743.

check.q: What were mufflers?
check.why: Broughton used padded gloves called mufflers for practice, not for prize fights.

check.q: How much time did Broughton's rules give a fallen boxer?
check.why: One of Broughton's rules gave a fallen boxer 30 seconds to come back to the middle.

lessons.title: The Last Bare-Knuckle Title
lessons.mainIdea: Under the London Prize Ring Rules, fights had no set length; the last bare-knuckle heavyweight title fight in 1889 went 75 rounds.
reading: In 1838, English boxing adopted new rules called the *London Prize Ring Rules*. They replaced Broughton's rules. A round ended whenever a boxer went down. There was no limit on the number of rounds. Fights could last for hours.

Prize fights were illegal in many American states. Fans rode special trains to secret places so police could not stop the fight. On July 8, 1889, John L. Sullivan fought Jake Kilrain near Richburg, Mississippi. They fought with bare fists in the summer heat.

Sullivan won after 75 rounds. It was the last heavyweight *championship* fought with bare knuckles under London rules. Mississippi later charged Sullivan for breaking its law against prize fighting. After this, top boxers moved to gloves and the Queensberry Rules.

words.d: bare-knuckle boxing rules adopted in England in 1838, with no limit on rounds
a contest to decide who holds a title as the best

check.q: Why did fans ride trains to secret places?
choices: prize fights were illegal in many states

check.why: Prize fighting broke the law in many states, so fights were held where police could not easily stop them.

lessons.title: Who Wrote Queensberry
lessons.mainIdea: John Graham Chambers wrote the Queensberry Rules; the Marquess of Queensberry lent them his name in 1867.
reading: The rules carry the name of John Sholto Douglas, the ninth *Marquess* of Queensberry. A marquess is a high-ranking noble in Britain. He was a young sports fan who backed the new rules and gave cups as prizes.

The man who wrote the rules was John Graham Chambers. He was a Welsh sportsman who had rowed at Cambridge University. In 1866 he helped start the *Amateur* Athletic Club in London. It held contests for people who did not compete for money.

The rules were published in 1867. They were meant for amateur contests with gloves. Over the next 25 years, professional boxers took them up too. People still call boxing's basic rules the Queensberry Rules.

words.d: a high-ranking noble title in Britain
a person who takes part in a sport without being paid
a person who is paid to take part in a sport

look.title: Name on the Cover, Writer Inside

look.prompt: Why might a new set of rules carry a famous person's name instead of the writer's name?

check.q: What is an amateur?

check.why: An amateur takes part in a sport without being paid, like the members of Chambers's club.

check.q: What club did Chambers help start in 1866?
check.why: Chambers helped start the Amateur Athletic Club in London in 1866.

lessons.title: Twelve Short Rules
lessons.mainIdea: The Queensberry Rules set three-minute rounds, a one-minute rest, a ten-second count and gloves.
reading: The Queensberry Rules had just twelve short rules. They set each *round* at three minutes. They gave one minute of rest between rounds. They banned wrestling and hugging in the ring.

A fallen boxer now had ten seconds to get up, not 30. If he could not, the other boxer won. Rule 10 asked for fair-sized gloves of the best quality. Under older rules, a round could last a few seconds or many minutes.

The clock changed boxing. Rounds of equal length made bouts easier to follow and to judge. Gloves made the bare-knuckle prize fight look old. Most boxing rules today still use three-minute rounds for men.

words.d: one part of a boxing bout, set by a clock, with rest in between
twelve boxing rules published in London in 1867, with gloves and three-minute rounds

look.title: Rule 3

look.cite: Queensberry Rules, London, 1867, Rule 3 (retold in plain English)
look.prompt: How is this rule different from the London Prize Ring Rules, where a round ended when a boxer went down?

check.q: How long was a round under the Queensberry Rules?
check.why: Rule 3 set each round at three minutes, with a minute of rest.

check.q: How long did a fallen boxer have to get up under Queensberry?
check.why: The Queensberry Rules cut the time from Broughton's 30 seconds to ten seconds.

check.q: What did the Queensberry Rules ban in the ring?
check.why: The rules banned wrestling and hugging, keeping the contest to boxing.

lessons.title: Gloves Win the Title
lessons.mainIdea: In 1892 in New Orleans, James J. Corbett beat John L. Sullivan in a heavyweight title fight with gloves under Queensberry Rules.
reading: On September 7, 1892, John L. Sullivan fought James J. Corbett at the Olympic Club in New Orleans, Louisiana. Both men wore gloves. They fought under the Queensberry Rules, with three-minute rounds.

Sullivan was the famous bare-knuckle champion. Corbett was a former bank clerk from San Francisco. Newspapers called him Gentleman Jim. Corbett won in the 21st round and became the heavyweight champion.

The fight was held indoors, under electric lights, before a paying crowd. It was legal in New Orleans. The fight showed that a big title could be won with gloves, rounds and a *referee* under Queensberry Rules.

words.d: the class for the biggest boxers; its champion was the most famous title
the official in the ring who makes sure boxers follow the rules

look.title: Two Title Fights
look.text: 1889: outdoors near Richburg, Mississippi, in the summer sun. Bare fists. No limit on rounds. Against state law. 1892: indoors in New Orleans, under electric lights. Gloves. Three-minute rounds. A legal event with tickets.
look.prompt: List three changes between the two fights. Which change do you think mattered most?

check.why: Corbett beat Sullivan in the 21st round in New Orleans in 1892.

check.q: Under which rules was the 1892 fight held?
check.why: Sullivan and Corbett wore gloves and fought under the Queensberry Rules.

check.q: What is a referee?
choices: the official who makes sure boxers follow the rules
check.why: The referee is the official in the ring who enforces the rules.

lessons.title: Amateur Boxing and the Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Amateur boxing got its own governing bodies and joined the modern Olympics in 1904; women's boxing joined in 2012.
reading: In 1880, the Amateur Boxing Association was founded in England. It was a *governing body*, a group that writes rules and runs championships. It held national amateur championships with gloves and short bouts.

Boxing joined the modern Olympic Games in 1904, in St. Louis, Missouri. All the boxers that year were from the United States. Olympic boxers were amateurs. Over the years, Olympic boxing added weight classes and new rules for safety.

Women boxed in exhibitions long before they could win Olympic medals. Women's boxing first joined the Olympics in 2012, in London. Nicola Adams of Great Britain won the first women's Olympic boxing gold medal, in the flyweight class.

words.d: a group that writes the rules for a sport and runs its championships
a group of boxers of about the same body weight who box each other

check.why: Boxing joined the modern Olympics in 1904, in St. Louis.

check.why: A governing body, like the Amateur Boxing Association, writes rules and runs championships.

check.q: When did women's boxing first join the Olympics?
check.why: Women's boxing joined the Olympics in London in 2012.

lessons.title: Golden Gloves in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Newspapers started Golden Gloves tournaments for amateur boxers in the late 1920s, and Chicago's became one of the best known.
reading: In 1927, the New York Daily News started an amateur boxing tournament called the *Golden Gloves*. Winners got a small golden glove charm. The next year, the Chicago Tribune ran its own Golden Gloves in Chicago.

Arch Ward, the Tribune's sports editor, helped run the Chicago tournament. Boxers came from Chicago neighborhoods, from towns in Illinois and from nearby states. Champions from Chicago and New York then met in an intercity match.

The Golden Gloves did not belong to schools. A newspaper ran it, and clubs and gyms trained the boxers. It gave young amateurs a place to compete close to home. Many later professional champions started in Golden Gloves bouts.

words.d: amateur boxing tournaments first run by newspapers in New York (1927) and Chicago (1928)
a set of matches that ends with champions

look.title: Who Runs the Tournament?

look.prompt: Why might a newspaper want to run a boxing tournament? What did the gyms get from it?

check.q: Which newspaper started the Golden Gloves in 1927?
check.why: The New York Daily News started the Golden Gloves in 1927; the Chicago Tribune followed a year later.

check.q: Who trained the Golden Gloves boxers?
check.why: A newspaper ran the tournament, and clubs and gyms trained the boxers.

check.q: What did Golden Gloves winners receive?

check.why: Winners got a small golden glove charm, which gave the tournament its name.

lessons.title: College Boxing Ends
lessons.mainIdea: The NCAA held college boxing championships from 1932 to 1960 and stopped after a Wisconsin boxer died.
reading: The *NCAA*, the National Collegiate Athletic Association, runs college sports championships. It held its first national boxing championships in 1932. For almost 30 years, college boxing drew big crowds. The University of Wisconsin had one of the strongest teams.

In April 1960, the NCAA boxing championships were held in Madison, Wisconsin. A Wisconsin boxer named Charlie Mohr was hurt in his final bout. He died several days later. His death shocked his school and the nation.
The University of Wisconsin ended its boxing team. The NCAA voted to stop its boxing championships after 1960. Today some colleges have boxing clubs run by students. They are clubs, not NCAA teams.

words.d: the National Collegiate Athletic Association, which runs many college sports championships
a sport run by students or members rather than as an official school team

look.title: A Team or a Club?
look.text: Before 1960, a college boxer wore the school's colors at an NCAA championship. Today, a college boxer may join a club that students run. The club finds its own coach and its own bouts, outside the NCAA.
look.prompt: What changed for college boxers after 1960? Why might a college choose a club instead of a team?

check.q: What does NCAA stand for?
check.why: The NCAA is the National Collegiate Athletic Association.

check.q: What happened after Charlie Mohr died in 1960?

check.why: After Mohr's death, Wisconsin dropped boxing and the NCAA ended its championships after 1960.

check.q: How is college boxing run today?
check.why: Some colleges have boxing clubs run by students, not NCAA teams.
